ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The procedure for this study was approved by the University of British Columbia's behavioral research ethics board (BREB H24-00265).
Participants provided written informed consent before starting the experiment.
In total, 107 participants were recruited for the study.

Four participants did not meet the eligibility criteria on arrival at the lab session, and three participants experienced problems with the physiological data recordings, e.g., electrode detachment during testing (for more details, see the lab notebook on https://osf.io/ykcaj).
table.formatted: Four participants did not meet the eligibility criteria on arrival at the lab session, and three participants experienced problems with the physiological data recordings, e.g., electrode detachment during testing (for more details, see the lab notebook on <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/ykcaj">https://osf.io/ykcaj</ref>).

table.text: Thus, in total 100 participants were included in the analyses; European or white and 'don't know/don't want to indicate').
Interested participants were able to click on a link to get to an eligibility form, from which eligible participants were invited to an in-lab session.
After the task, participants filled in a post experimental survey including the craving item.

Lastly, participants completed a measure that we are not reporting here but a description of the task and the related analyses can be found in the supplementary materials (https://osf.io/smcau/files/qsmuj).
table.formatted: Lastly, participants completed a measure that we are not reporting here but a description of the task and the related analyses can be found in the supplementary materials (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/smcau/files/qsmuj">https://osf.io/smcau/files/qsmuj</ref>).

table.text: After each outcome phase, participants were presented with the arousal scale from the self-assessment manikin (httpshttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?NsbSAr//www.zotero.org/google-docs/?NsbSAr Bradley & Lang, 1994) : they indicated their current experienced arousal by clicking on the corresponding image of the SAM.
table.formatted: After each outcome phase, participants were presented with the arousal scale from the self-assessment manikin (<ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?NsbSAr">SAM;</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bradley & Lang, 1994)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?NsbSAr">:</ref> they indicated their current experienced arousal by clicking on the corresponding image of the SAM.

table.text: Participants were told that if they finished the game with any money that exceeded their initial endowment, this would be paid out as a bonus, although in using a fixed outcome sequence that was representative of a commercial 'house edge', no participants received a bonus.
Participants were compensated $22.50 for a 90 minute session.
In preparing for psychophysiology recording, participants were asked to wash their hands (without soap).

This task includes two blocks in which participants are instructed to only tap when they are sure they can feel their heartbeat (see supplementary materials https://osf.io/smcau/files/qsmuj) and in our study, roughly a quarter of participants never tapped in those blocks.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: We report data from a sample of 100 participants with usable data. Due to time and resource limitations, community recruitment was limited to 100 participants. A sensitivity analysis conducted with g*power (Faul et al., 2007) based on 1-ß = 0.8, a sample size of N = 100, alpha = 0.05, number of measurements = 2 (physiology and PGSI) and correlation between the repeated measures = 0.5 for an ANOVA with repeated measures indicates that our sample size was sufficient to detect a medium effect size f= 0.14.

report: We used the LLM model 'vllm/DeepSeek-V41-Flash-1017-FP8' to check the contents of 2 paragraphs that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses. All essential information could be detected. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(power_type = "sensitivity", statistical_test = "other", sample_size = 100, alpha_level = 0.05, power = 0.8, effect_size = 0.14, effect_size_metric = "Cohen's f", software = "G*Power"), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(text = "We report data from a sample of 100 participants with usable data. Due to time and resource limitations, community recruitment was limited to 100 participants. A sensitivity analysis conducted with g*power (Faul et al., 2007) based on 1-ß = 0.8, a sample size of N = 100, alpha = 0.05, number of measurements = 2 (physiology and PGSI) and correlation between the repeated measures = 0.5 for an ANOVA with repeated measures indicates that our sample size was sufficient to detect a medium effect size f= 0.14."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size. For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like: > An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group. For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like: > A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. ownership.dep_title: The interplay of subjective and objective measures of arousal during simulated gambling in a community sample with gambling involvement
ownership.dep_description: Verdejo-Garcia and colleagues (2012) developed an interoceptive-deficit hypothesis in addiction which we might be able to apply to gambling contexts by testing the coupling of physiological responses to gambling episodes with the subjective reports of these physiological responses. Here we specifically assume that the coupling of those measures changes as a function of gambling involvement. We assume that all participants will show larger mean changes in subjective experience and arousal responses to wins compared to losses. However, we predict that there will be a decoupling of physiological arousal and subjective ratings as a function of gambling involvement. This interoceptive deficit may thus contribute to more persistent gambling (i.e. loss chasing) based on perceived excitement. If we find support for this hypothesis, we further predict that losses, as an aversive outcome, will promote the decoupling between physiological arousal and subjective ratings: the more gambling invol...

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 144 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: The procedure for this study was approved by the University of British Columbia's behavioral research ethics board (BREB H24-00265).
live_data_statements: Participants provided written informed consent before starting the experiment.
In total, 107 participants were recruited for the study.

Four participants did not meet the eligibility criteria on arrival at the lab session, and three participants experienced problems with the physiological data recordings, e.g., electrode detachment during testing (for more details, see the lab notebook on https://osf.io/ykcaj).
Thus, in total 100 participants were included in the analyses; European or white and 'don't know/don't want to indicate').
Interested participants were able to click on a link to get to an eligibility form, from which eligible participants were invited to an in-lab session.
After the task, participants filled in a post experimental survey including the craving item.

Lastly, participants completed a measure that we are not reporting here but a description of the task and the related analyses can be found in the supplementary materials (https://osf.io/smcau/files/qsmuj).

After each outcome phase, participants were presented with the arousal scale from the self-assessment manikin (httpshttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?NsbSAr//www.zotero.org/google-docs/?NsbSAr Bradley & Lang, 1994) : they indicated their current experienced arousal by clicking on the corresponding image of the SAM.

Participants were told that if they finished the game with any money that exceeded their initial endowment, this would be paid out as a bonus, although in using a fixed outcome sequence that was representative of a commercial 'house edge', no participants received a bonus.
Participants were compensated $22.50 for a 90 minute session.
In preparing for psychophysiology recording, participants were asked to wash their hands (without soap).

This task includes two blocks in which participants are instructed to only tap when they are sure they can feel their heartbeat (see supplementary materials https://osf.io/smcau/files/qsmuj) and in our study, roughly a quarter of participants never tapped in those blocks.

**Undefined-variable errors**

**1 script failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. text.text: Objective: Psychological theories of gambling have traditionally emphasized arousal as a key source of reinforcement in the development and maintenance of problematic gambling behavior.
However, the exact role of arousal in excessive gambling remains unclear.

Past work has focused on physiological signals (e.g. heart rate and electrodermal activity change) without considering the subjective perception and interpretation of these signals from an interoceptive perspective.

The present study investigated the relationship between trial-by-trial subjective (self-assessment manikin) and objective (electrodermal activity and heart rate) measures of arousal, while participants played a slot machine task.

Method: A community sample with slot machine gambling experience (N = 100, PGSI scores 0-7), played a simulated slot machine task with concurrent recording of electrodermal activity (EDA) and heart rate.
After each trial, participants indicated their perceived arousal using a selfassessment manikin (SAM).
Results: We found higher subjective measures of arousal (SAM scores) and higher EDA peak amplitudes for wins compared to losses.
We found a trial-by-trial relationship between objective and the SAM subjective measures of arousal for EDA peak amplitude, but not for HR.
We found no support for the hypothesis that this relationship is influenced by PGSI scores.
Discussion: Despite evidence of coupling between subjective and objective measures of arousal during gambling, a relationship with gambling severity was not supported.

This highlights the need to further implement interoceptive methodologies to examine the perception and appraisal of arousal in gambling situations to explain the role of arousal and interoception of arousal in the development of excessive gambling behavior.

Theories of emotion and cognition agree that emotions and their physiological responses (i.e. arousal) play an important role in decision making processes (Clore & Huntsinger, 2007; Damasio et al., 1996; Dunn et al., 2010; Frijda, 2010).
text.formatted: Theories of emotion and cognition agree that emotions and their physiological responses (i.e. arousal) play an important role in decision making processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Clore & Huntsinger, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Damasio et al., 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Dunn et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Frijda, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In order to take these physiological responses into account in decision making, individuals must be able to subjectively experience them.

Based on the idea that gambling problems might be explained by abnormalities in arousal levels (Baudinet & Blaszczynski, 2013; Blaszczynski & Nower, 2002; Nower et al., 2022; Sharpe, 2002), the current study tested whether the subjective experience of arousal, and its objective physiological counterparts covary with one another, and whether this relationship was 'decoupled' as a function of problem gambling severity (Ferris & Wynne, 2001).
text.formatted: Based on the idea that gambling problems might be explained by abnormalities in arousal levels <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Baudinet & Blaszczynski, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Blaszczynski & Nower, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Nower et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Sharpe, 2002)</ref>, the current study tested whether the subjective experience of arousal, and its objective physiological counterparts covary with one another, and whether this relationship was 'decoupled' as a function of problem gambling severity <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Ferris & Wynne, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Gambling is commonly portrayed as a recreational activity, but a subset of people who gamble encounter significant harmful consequences (see Wardle et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Gambling is commonly portrayed as a recreational activity, but a subset of people who gamble encounter significant harmful consequences (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Wardle et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: It is well established that engagement in gambling is accompanied by increased physiological arousal, such as increasing heart rate or electrodermal activity (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?roXdZc  Baudinet & Blaszczynski, 2013 https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?roXdZc  Coventry & Constable, 1999; Wulfert et al., 2008).
text.formatted: It is well established that engagement in gambling is accompanied by increased physiological arousal, such as increasing heart rate or electrodermal activity (<ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?roXdZc">EDA,</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Baudinet & Blaszczynski, 2013</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?roXdZc">for a review;</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Coventry & Constable, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Wulfert et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: These experiences of arousal are thought to be a key source of reinforcement in gambling behavior, but it is not clear whether this mechanism is driven by hyper-or hypo-arousal responses (e.g., Baudinet & Blaszczynski, 2013; Blaszczynski & Nower, 2002; Nower et al., 2022; Sharpe, 2002).
text.formatted: These experiences of arousal are thought to be a key source of reinforcement in gambling behavior, but it is not clear whether this mechanism is driven by hyper-or hypo-arousal responses (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Baudinet & Blaszczynski, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Blaszczynski & Nower, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Nower et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Sharpe, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Despite its appeal, evidence for this arousal framework still provides a limited explanation as to why only some people experience problems in relation to their gambling: the physiological correlates of these emotional responses have not reliably differentiated those with and without gambling problems.

In addition to several methodological limitations, including the use of small samples, inconsistent screening for problematic gambling, and potentially noisy ambulatory recordings, the literature has focused almost exclusively on physiological arousal at the signal level.
Yet, no reliable and replicable physiological pattern has emerged that distinguishes or predicts problematic versus nonproblematic gambling.
We argue that this may be because the physiological signal represents only one part of the process.
The critical individual differences may lie not in the magnitude of physiological responses per se, but in how these responses are perceived, interpreted, and integrated into subsequent behaviour.

Interoceptionhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?mvDAi6 i.e. the perception and interpretation of internal bodily signals (Desmedt et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?YyXNgS 2024) , is a multidimensional construct which encompasses several domains, including the perception of cardiac, visceral and gastrointestinal signals (Suksasilp & Garfinkel, 2022) , and operates across several hierarchical levels from the afferent signal level (e.g., physiological arousal) to the central representation (e.g., neural representation and interoceptive accuracy) and finally, higher-order measures such as attention to physiological signals and meta-cognitive beliefs about interoception (e.g., attribution of interoceptive states, interoceptive insight, or self-report and interoceptive beliefs).
text.formatted: Interoception, i.e. the perception and interpretation of internal bodily signals <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Desmedt et al., 2024)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?mvDAi6">,</ref> is a multidimensional construct which encompasses several domains, including the perception of cardiac, visceral and gastrointestinal signals <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Suksasilp & Garfinkel, 2022)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?YyXNgS">,</ref> and operates across several hierarchical levels from the afferent signal level (e.g., physiological arousal) to the central representation (e.g., neural representation and interoceptive accuracy) and finally, higher-order measures such as attention to physiological signals and meta-cognitive beliefs about interoception (e.g., attribution of interoceptive states, interoceptive insight, or self-report and interoceptive beliefs).

text.text: There has been much recent interest in interoception in the context of mental health (Greenwood & Garfinkelhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?5m521N 2025; Khalsa et al., 2018) , including addictions (Lovelock et al., 2021; Paulus et al., 2009; Paulus & Stewart, 2014; Verdejo-Garcia et al., 2012).
text.formatted: There has been much recent interest in interoception in the context of mental health <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Greenwood & Garfinkel, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Khalsa et al., 2018)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?5m521N">,</ref> including addictions <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Lovelock et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Paulus et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Paulus & Stewart, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Verdejo-Garcia et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: In exploring the conceptual and empirical links between interoception and addiction, Verdejo-García, Clark, and Dunn (2012) proposed an 'interoceptive deficit' in addictive disorders, although at that time there was a lack of experimental evidence linking these processes.
text.formatted: In exploring the conceptual and empirical links between interoception and addiction, Verdejo-García, <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Clark, and Dunn (2012)</ref> proposed an 'interoceptive deficit' in addictive disorders, although at that time there was a lack of experimental evidence linking these processes.

text.text: A more recent conceptualization and evidence inventory focused primarily on substance addictions (Leganes-Fonteneau et al., under review) suggests that empirical progress has since remained modest.
text.formatted: A more recent conceptualization and evidence inventory focused primarily on substance addictions <ref type="bibr">(Leganes-Fonteneau et al., under review)</ref> suggests that empirical progress has since remained modest.

text.text: Moving the field forward requires going beyond a general deficit account by matching specific interoceptive constructs and measures with addiction-related processes in conceptually and empirically meaningful ways.

Gambling offers a particularly useful context for doing so, as its repeated cycles of anticipation, choice, and outcome allow physiological responses, subjective arousal, and behaviour to be assessed concurrently over multiple trials.

Unlike substance-use paradigms, where repeated drug administration is constrained, gambling tasks enable trial-by-trial examination of how physiological signals are translated into experienced arousal, and how this coupling shapes subsequent decisions and behavioural persistence.

In a previous study, Diskin and Hodgins (2003) investigated objective and subjective measures of arousal during authentic slot machine gambling as heart rate, skin conductance and facial electromyography were recorded.
text.formatted: In a previous study, <ref type="bibr">Diskin and Hodgins (2003)</ref> investigated objective and subjective measures of arousal during authentic slot machine gambling as heart rate, skin conductance and facial electromyography were recorded.

text.text: There were no significant differences in objective physiological measures between groups, but those who experienced problems reported to feel higher arousal levels than those who did not experience problems.

In that study, tonic physiological signals were averaged over periods of several minutes, and we reasoned that phasic measures of arousal might deliver a more granular measurement of the coupling between objective and subjective measures of arousal sensitive to win or loss outcomes.

The current study examines how objective measures of arousal are elicited by slot machine gambling events on a trial-by-trial basis, and how these responses are coupled with the subjective experience of arousal, in order to establish the role of interoception in the development and maintenance of problematic gambling behavior.

Here, objective arousal was measured using EDA and heart rate (HR) deceleration, and the subjective experience of arousal on each trial was measured with the self-assessment manikin (SAM; Bradley & Lang, 1994).
text.formatted: Here, objective arousal was measured using EDA and heart rate (HR) deceleration, and the subjective experience of arousal on each trial was measured with the self-assessment manikin (SAM; <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bradley & Lang, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: We focused on outcome-related activity (i.e. to wins or losses) as a moment that is associated with a robust, phasic emotional response.
We expected (and pre-registered) that the coupling of physiological arousal and subjective feelings of arousal during gambling would be attenuated in people with higher PGSI scores.
This could be potentially driven by higher perceived arousal when experiencing losses, compared to people with lower PGSI scores.

In this way, the dysregulation of interoceptive processing could explain more persistent gambling (i.e. loss chasing, continued gambling despite substantial losses to recover these losses) based on perceived excitement.
Hypotheses 1) Wins, compared to losses, would elicit greater HR deceleration, EDA peak amplitude, and subjective arousal measured by the SAM ratings.
2) People with higher PGSI scores would show reduced coupling between physiological and subjective measures of arousal.

2A) Conditional upon support for H2, we will explore whether losses promote this decoupling: i.e. with higher levels of problem gambling, we predicted greater self-reported arousal in response to losses, even though their physiological responses do not support these feelings.

text.text: In this manuscript, we report which analyses were preregistered and which analyses were added as exploratory analyses.
We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions, all manipulations, and all measures in the study.
The procedure for this study was approved by the University of British Columbia's behavioral research ethics board (BREB H24-00265).
Participants provided written informed consent before starting the experiment.
We ran a student pilot sample (N=52) as a precursor to this project.
We used this sample to determine outlier criteria and analysis steps with regard to the preprocessing of the psychophysiological data.
Those steps were determined in an exploratory manner.
All data, code and materials of this sample can be found in the folder 'Pilot Study -Student Sample' with this project on OSF (https://osf.io/smcau/).

text.text: We report data from a sample of 100 participants with usable data.
Due to time and resource limitations, community recruitment was limited to 100 participants.

A sensitivity analysis conducted with g*power (Faul et al., 2007) based on 1-ß = 0.8, a sample size of N = 100, alpha = 0.05, number of measurements = 2 (physiology and PGSI) and correlation between the repeated measures = 0.5 for an ANOVA with repeated measures indicates that our sample size was sufficient to detect a medium effect size f= 0.14.

text.text: In total, 107 participants were recruited for the study.

Four participants did not meet the eligibility criteria on arrival at the lab session, and three participants experienced problems with the physiological data recordings, e.g., electrode detachment during testing (for more details, see the lab notebook on https://osf.io/ykcaj).

text.text: Thus, in total 100 participants were included in the analyses; European or white and 'don't know/don't want to indicate').
Please note that the race/ethnicity is not shared in the raw data due to the risk of reidentification of participants.
We only included participants with a PGSI score of 0-7 (mean = 1.86), but our recruitment did not control further for group sizes within that range.

Eligibility criteria required participants to have prior experience playing slot machines (either online or in gambling venues) in the past three months (due to a procedural error, this deviates from the preregistered criterion 'on at least three occasions in the past 12 months'), but must not have had any gambling problems or treatment in the past (including 'self-exclusion programs').
General Procedure.
We advertised the study via facebook/instagram advertisements.
Interested participants were able to click on a link to get to an eligibility form, from which eligible participants were invited to an in-lab session.

On arrival at the lab, after filling in the consent form, participants repeated the eligibility screening, followed by a set of demographic questions (i.e, age, gender, cultural background, and ethnicity), and questionnaires that we will not report here but can be found in the raw data.
Before and after the behavioral tasks, we asked participants about their motive to gamble, and a gambling craving item to quantify whether the task induced any desire to gamble.

Following the questionnaire surveys, the psychophysiological sensors were affixed to the participants, with a resting period of 5 minutes of Biopac recording for signal stabilization, before commencing the computerized slot machine task.
After the task, participants filled in a post experimental survey including the craving item.

Lastly, participants completed a measure that we are not reporting here but a description of the task and the related analyses can be found in the supplementary materials (https://osf.io/smcau/files/qsmuj).

text.text: The entire procedure took about 90 minutes with about 20 minutes psychophysiological preparation time and about 60 minutes on the questionnaires and tasks.
Participants gambled on a realistic three-reel slot machine simulation as in Palmer et al. (2024).

text.text: This simulation was designed using Custom Slots Framework 1.4 with Unity 2018 4.29 (LaFrontier, 2018; Unity Technologies, 2018).

text.text: We used the same outcome sequences as programmed by Palmer et al. (2024) in which the slot machine simulation returned three possible outcome types: wins (1/6 of trials), full-misses (3/6 of trials), and near-misses (2/6 of trials), delivered over 120 trials.

(2024)</ref> in which the slot machine simulation returned three possible outcome types: wins (1/6 of trials), full-misses (3/6 of trials), and near-misses (2/6 of trials), delivered over 120 trials.

text.text: Our analysis plan focussed on the binary classification of wins versus losses (i.e. near-misses and full-misses); over 120 trials.
The participant received 20 wins and 100 losses.
Wins were accompanied by audiovisual feedback in which each winning symbol rotated, and a short jingle played for 1 s.
Loss outcomes were not celebrated with any audiovisual feedback.
Each trial was six seconds long.
After participants pressed the spin button, the three reels started spinning: after 1 s, the first reel stopped, after 2s, the second reel stopped, and after 3 s, the third reel stopped.
The outcome was presented for 3 s.

After each outcome phase, participants were presented with the arousal scale from the self-assessment manikin (httpshttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?NsbSAr//www.zotero.org/google-docs/?NsbSAr  Bradley & Lang, 1994) : they indicated their current experienced arousal by clicking on the corresponding image of the SAM.
text.formatted: After each outcome phase, participants were presented with the arousal scale from the self-assessment manikin (<ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?NsbSAr">SAM;</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bradley & Lang, 1994)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?NsbSAr">:</ref> they indicated their current experienced arousal by clicking on the corresponding image of the SAM.

text.text: The SAM rating and ensuing spin initiation latency (SIL) were self-paced by the participants.
Each participant was provided with a 4000-credit endowment at the start of the task.
The bet size was fixed at 10 credits, where 1 credit is equal to CAD $0.01.
A win returned 5x the initial bet size (i.e., 10 credit bet = 50 credit win).

Participants were told that if they finished the game with any money that exceeded their initial endowment, this would be paid out as a bonus, although in using a fixed outcome sequence that was representative of a commercial 'house edge', no participants received a bonus.
Participants were compensated $22.50 for a 90 minute session.
During the task, EDA and HR data (via electrocardiogram) was acquired via a Biopac MP150 at a sampling frequency of 2,000 Hz.
For the recording of EDA, we used the wireless PPGED-R; for HR, we used the RSPEC-R amplifiers.
The basic setup involved 3 hardware components: a stimulus delivery computer that presented the task, a recording computer that was operated by the researcher, and the Biopac system.
The stimulus delivery computer was connected to the Biopac via a serial port cable (USB TTL Module provided by Biopac).
The recording computer was connected to the Biopac via an ethernet cable.

During the two tasks, the various psychological events (e.g. the participant's response, the delivery of the gamble outcome) were marked on the psychophysiology record in Acqknowledge (version 5.0) using triggers sent via serial port.
In preparing for psychophysiology recording, participants were asked to wash their hands (without soap).
The research assistant attached two disposable EDA electrodes to the fingertips of the index and middle fingers of the non-dominant hand.
For the electrocardiogram, we attached three electrodes to the right wrist and both ankles.

Preprocessing of physiological data (for all analyses described above) was done with the Neurokit2 toolkit (Makowski et al., 2021) in Python (the detailed descriptions of the methods can be found in the Neurokit2 documentation: https://neuropsychology.github.io/NeuroKit/).
text.formatted: Preprocessing of physiological data (for all analyses described above) was done with the Neurokit2 toolkit <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Makowski et al., 2021)</ref> in Python (the detailed descriptions of the methods can be found in the Neurokit2 documentation: <ref type="url" target="https://neuropsychology.github.io/NeuroKit/">https://neuropsychology.github.io/NeuroKit/</ref>).

text.text: For preprocessing the HR data, we first cleaned the signal to remove noise and improve peak detection accuracy.
The cleaning function uses a 0.5 Hz high-pass butterworth filter followed by powerline filtering (powerline = 50).
Then the HR signal quality was assessed.
Next, Neurokit2 finds R-peaks in the electrocardiogram signal using a function to delineate the QRS complex, i.e., the component waves of the cardiac cycles.
Neurokit2 then computes cardiac phase (for both atrial and ventricular), and the signal rate was calculated from the series of peaks.
This is a general function that works for any series of peaks (i.e., not specific to cardiac signals).
It is computed as 60 / period, where the period is the time between the peaks.
For EDA, we cleaned the signal by removing noise and smoothing the signal with different methods.
Next, Neurokit2 decomposes the EDA recording into Phasic and Tonic components, using Biopac's Acqknowledge algorithms.

The default high-pass decomposition in neurokit2 lead to about ⅙ of the trials having negative values for the EDA peak amplitude, which are implausible values, and therefore we used the smoothmedian method for decomposition of the EDA, which was not preregistered.

To reduce the amount of computing power required for the different decompositions in the EDA analyses, we decided to down-sampled the EDA signal to 128 Hz for the preprocessing, but we resampled to 2000 Hz for the epoch analyses.

In the psychophysiological data, we excluded trials in which the mean HR was below 40 bpm or above 150 bpm (0.01% of all trials), which were considered implausible values for a seated laboratory test.
We measured subjective arousal with the SAM, and EDA and HR deceleration as measures of objective arousal.

In a deviation from the preregistration, we were not able to analyze spin initiation latencies as a behavioral measure, because the SAM decision times occupied a variable length during the initiation interval.
For the EDA data, we calculated the average EDA peak amplitude for the time 3 s after the outcome presentation.
For the HR deceleration, we took the 3 s reel spin on each trial as a baseline, and the 3 s outcome presentation as our epoch of interest.

We calculated the average HR for each baseline and subtracted the HR minima in the outcome epoch from the baseline (see Hultmann et al., 2022), to form the HR deceleration score, which we then compared between win and loss trials.
text.formatted: We calculated the average HR for each baseline and subtracted the HR minima in the outcome epoch from the baseline (see <ref type="bibr">Hultmann et al., 2022)</ref>, to form the HR deceleration score, which we then compared between win and loss trials.

text.text: For establishing data quality and to test our first hypothesis, we conducted (non-preregistered) oneway ANOVAs and follow-up two-sided t-tests to test the difference in the SAM scores, EDA peak amplitude and HR deceleration following wins vs. losses with a Bonferroni correction of alpha for multiple testing (alpha = .05/3 = .017).
We predicted wins (which were also the rarer of the two outcomes) would elicit higher SAM scores, higher EDA peak amplitudes, and greater HR deceleration.

To test whether there is a relationship between the subjective (SAM ratings) and objective (EDA peak amplitude and HR deceleration) measures, two separate trial-by-trial Pearson correlational analyses tested the relationship between the SAM score and the EDA peak amplitude of the corresponding trial, and the relationship between SAM response score and the HR deceleration of the corresponding trial.
A correlation coefficient was obtained using the trial-bytrial data across all participants.

We preregistered that we would combine EDA and HR deceleration into one compound score by averaging their respective within-subject z-scores, expecting EDA and HR deceleration were significantly correlated on a trial-by-trial level.

Despite a significant correlation, the effect size of this correlation was numerically very small (r= -.026), suggesting that in this dataset, EDA and HR reflected complementary facets of physiological arousal (https://osf.io/smcau/files/qsmuj); the preregistered analysis is reported in the supplementary materials.
text.formatted: Despite a significant correlation, the effect size of this correlation was numerically very small (r= -.026), suggesting that in this dataset, EDA and HR reflected complementary facets of physiological arousal (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/smcau/files/qsmuj">https://osf.io/smcau/files/qsmuj</ref>); the preregistered analysis is reported in the supplementary materials.

text.text: Lastly, to test our main hypothesis whether problem gambling severity (continuous PGSI score) predicts the strength of these relationships, we conducted two linear mixed effects models using restricted maximum likelihood (REML) to account for repeated measures and individual differences.
We ran two models, one EDA peak amplitudes, and HR deceleration, both including random intercepts and random slopes to capture the variability in these two signals across participants.
We used the following model specification (with Physio referring to either EDA peak amplitude or HR deceleration): SAM ~ Physio * PGSI + (1 | ParticipantID).
Our fixed main effects were the physiological measure (EDA peak amplitude or HR deceleration), and PGSI score.
We also tested the two-way interactions between the physiological measures and PGSI score.
In this way, we determined if the relationship between physiology measures and SAM response scores is influenced by PGSI score (gambling severity).
We also re-ran the outcome-related analyses, coding near-misses as a discrete type of loss (see Clark et al 2009 , Paliwal & Petzschner 2014).

The difference between near-misses (M = 3.83 bpm, SD = 1.09) and losses was not significant, t(99) = 1.31, p = 0.193, or between near-misses and wins, t(99) = 2.08, p = 0.04.
Therefore, we only observed a clear, significant near miss effect on SAM and EDA, and not on HR deceleration.

This study examined whether the trial-by-trial coupling between the subjective experience of arousal and the physiological response is altered among people with higher PGSI scores, as an expression of interoceptive dysregulation.

Participants gambled on a computerized slot machine task and indicated their perceived arousal on the SAM after each outcome, as a subjective measure of arousal that was correlated on a trial-by-trial basis against EDA and HR deceleration as objective measures of arousal.

In line with our predictions and previous literature (Coventry & Constablehttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?JRkyZX 1999; Diskin et al., 2003; Diskin & Hodgins, 2003; Moodie & Finnigan, 2005) , we found that wins elicited significantly higher EDA and SAM ratings than losses, and these measures co-varied on the trial-by-trial level, with higher EDA peak amplitudes fluctuating with higher SAM ratings.
text.formatted: In line with our predictions and previous literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Coventry & Constable, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Diskin et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Diskin & Hodgins, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Moodie & Finnigan, 2005)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?JRkyZX">,</ref> we found that wins elicited significantly higher EDA and SAM ratings than losses, and these measures co-varied on the trial-by-trial level, with higher EDA peak amplitudes fluctuating with higher SAM ratings.

text.text: Interestingly, losses produced significantly larger HR deceleration than wins, and HR deceleration covaried negatively with SAM ratings.
PGSI score did not influence any of these effects, suggesting no influence of gambling severity on the relationship between objective and subjective measures of arousal.

This study constitutes useful proof-of-concept data that moment-to-moment mapping of interoceptive processes is possible in the context of gambling by looking at trial-by-trial fluctuations in these responses.
Participants with varying levels of problem gambling are able to report their moment to moment physiological states.
Nevertheless, there is no support for our hypothesis that this trial-by-trial relationship is influenced by PGSI scores.

One possibility is that other interoceptive processes such as the interoceptive attribution, belief insight, or phenomenology (i.e. the characteristics of the internal bodily sensations; Desmedt et al., 2025) might play a bigger role in the development and maintenance of problematic gambling behavior than the moment to moment subjective experience of arousal.
text.formatted: One possibility is that other interoceptive processes such as the interoceptive attribution, belief insight, or phenomenology (i.e. the characteristics of the internal bodily sensations; <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Desmedt et al., 2025)</ref> might play a bigger role in the development and maintenance of problematic gambling behavior than the moment to moment subjective experience of arousal.

text.text: Future studies can thus investigate different interoceptive levels in gambling with a trial-by-trial set up and may include preclinical and clinical samples.
The complexity of these physiological signals is noteworthy, especially the biphasic nature of event-related HR changes in fast-paced psychological tasks.

Originally, objective measures of arousal such as HR deceleration and EDA were characterized in static situations with emotional cues such as pictures from the International Affective Picture System (IAPS, (Bradley et al., 2001; Bradley & Lang, 2000).

text.text: Our slot machine task is faster paced, and the anticipatory intervals of the reel spin introduce a further element of reward dynamics, making the physiological responses more complex to investigate.

As shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3, both HR and EDA signals begin to change before the moment of outcome delivery, likely because the symbol matches across the first and second reels on winning outcomes (which occur 1 and 2 seconds into each anticipatory epoch) instil an expectancy of winning.

text.text: Anticipatory processing is often accompanied by the physiological reactivity (Agren, 2023; Herman et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Anticipatory processing is often accompanied by the physiological reactivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Agren, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Herman et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, we are not able to fully disentangle which effects are driven by anticipation from those of outcome presentation.

The baseline epoch for calculating HR deceleration includes this anticipatory component, and in using fast-paced the task to maintain ecological validity of slot machine gambling, this was the only viable option for determining the baseline signal.

When adding near-misses as a special kind of loss (Clark et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?95m2yl 2013; Dixon et al., 2011) , near-misses elicited higher subjective arousal and EDA than full-misses, albeit at levels lower than the equivalent responses to winning outcomes.

text.text: On HR deceleration, there was a greater signal for losses compared to wins, but no effects of near misses.

Earlier studies have found that near-misses elicit increases in EDA and HR reactivity (Dixon et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?m3mKIq 2011 , Clark et al., 2012 , Clark et al., 2013) , and we were only able to replicate these findings for EDA.

text.text: Our findings are also in line with Palmer et al. (2024) who found that near-misses yield intermediate responses between wins and losses on self-reported motivation and valence.

text.text: One question that remains unanswered is what aspect of interoception is being measured by the coupling between phasic physiological responses and self-reported SAM ratings of arousal.

On the one hand, it is possible that physiological arousal represents the interoceptive signal (Desmedt et al., 2024 https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?HXlhE1 yet it remains unclear at which level of analysis (e.g., interoceptive detection, accuracy or magnitude) the subjective experience of arousal occurs, or which level of interoception this coupling represents.
text.formatted: On the one hand, it is possible that physiological arousal represents the interoceptive signal <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Desmedt et al., 2024</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?HXlhE1">),</ref> yet it remains unclear at which level of analysis (e.g., interoceptive detection, accuracy or magnitude) the subjective experience of arousal occurs, or which level of interoception this coupling represents.

text.text: While the measurement of SAM arousal ratings are intended to be a language free and valence free measure, we cannot exclude that the way we asked participants about their subjective experience ('Click on the manikin that best matched your level of emotional intensity for the outcome you just experienced') might have influenced their responses.
It is possible that the depiction of 'emotional intensity' via the SAM carried some sort of valence meaning for the participants and influenced their rating.

More likely, the experience of arousal is a result of multiple processes that may involve more than the pure "intensity" of emotion but also some evaluation of the outcome (i.e., valence) and other appraisal processes.

In summary, it is possible that the subjective experience of arousal measured with the SAM does not represent one level of interoception but is influenced by multiple levels to form together the subjective experience of arousal.
We would like to highlight that some methodological properties of our task and design might have influenced some of our conclusions.

The hypothesis that people with higher PGSI scores show a less close coupling of subjective and objective measures of arousal may have been compromised by a degree by the range restriction on the PGSI, due to the ethical considerations of not exposing people with higher scores (> 7) to a slot machine simulator.
text.formatted: The hypothesis that people with higher PGSI scores show a less close coupling of subjective and objective measures of arousal may have been compromised by a degree by the range restriction on the PGSI, due to the ethical considerations of not exposing people with higher scores (> 7) to a slot machine simulator.

text.text: Conceivably, we may have found evidence for moderation in a sample with a wider range on the PGSI or a greater number of people with at-risk or problematic levels of gambling.
Additionally, the PGSI distribution was highly skewed with roughly ⅓ of our sample having a PGSI of 0.

Second, our three reel task did not closely emulate modern slot machine design, which would typically feature multi-line play, high reinforcement rates, bonus games, and various other features that likely fuel arousal.
Lastly, the insertion of a trial-by-trial SAM rating is unrealistic and may have likely disrupted immersive states that typically characterize slot machine use (Murch et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Lastly, the insertion of a trial-by-trial SAM rating is unrealistic and may have likely disrupted immersive states that typically characterize slot machine use <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Murch et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, research taking into account any interoceptive levels and measures in gambling research is scarce.
To our knowledge only two studies have attempted to investigate interoceptive accuracy in the context of problematic gambling (Kennedy et al., 2019; Moccia et al., 2021).
text.formatted: To our knowledge only two studies have attempted to investigate interoceptive accuracy in the context of problematic gambling <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Kennedy et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Moccia et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Both studies used the heartbeat counting task (Schandry, 1981) but their results point in different directions. Moccia et al (2021) found that individuals with GD exhibited significantly lower interoceptive accuracy than healthy controls, indicating a diminished ability to perceive internal bodily signals, but Kennedy et al (2019) observed no task-related differences in a GD group.
text.formatted: Both studies used the heartbeat counting task <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Schandry, 1981)</ref> but their results point in different directions. <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Moccia et al (2021)</ref> found that individuals with GD exhibited significantly lower interoceptive accuracy than healthy controls, indicating a diminished ability to perceive internal bodily signals, but <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Kennedy et al (2019)</ref> observed no task-related differences in a GD group.

text.text: However, these studies rely on a single measure of interoception in a specific domain (cardiac interoception), negating the rich multidimensionality of interoceptive processing (Leganes-Fonteneau et al.
Under Review), and the validity of the heart beat counting task itself has been heavily criticized (Billaux et al., 2025; Desmedt et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Under Review), and the validity of the heart beat counting task itself has been heavily criticized <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Billaux et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Desmedt et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In this project, we hoped to address these concerns by using the heartbeat tapping task (Smith et al., 2021) but we encountered high data loss in two blocks of the tapping task(https://osf.io/smcau/files/qsmuj).
text.formatted: In this project, we hoped to address these concerns by using the heartbeat tapping task <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Smith et al., 2021)</ref> but we encountered high data loss in two blocks of the tapping task(<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/smcau/files/qsmuj">https://osf.io/smcau/files/qsmuj</ref>).

text.text: Nevertheless, despite some limitations, the current study provides a new, more granular approach investigating the coupling of subjective and physiological measures of arousal.
This will allow us to examine different dimensions of interoception that could impact the perception of arousal.

In summary, we found that in participants with prior slot machine experience, the coupling of physiological and subjective arousal signals indicates accurate reporting of moment-to-moment changes in physiological arousal during slot machine gambling.
Importantly, we did not find any influence of problem gambling severity on this relationship.

These results do not support predictions from the interoceptive deficit hypothesis as applied to problematic gambling, and suggest that, at least in low to moderate risk gambling, interoceptive ability during simulated gambling is largely intact.
